q: Which English king was deposed in the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89?
explain: The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 saw James II deposed and replaced by his daughter Mary II and her husband William III, prince of Orange.
hook: James II went 'too far' and fled to France.

sources.title: Glorious Revolution | Britannica
sources.quote: Glorious Revolution , in English history, the events of 1688–89 that resulted in the deposition of James II and the accession of his daughter Mary II and her husband, William III , prince of Orange and stadholder of the United Provinces of the Netherlands .

sources.title: The Bill of Rights 1689 - House of Commons Library
sources.quote: The Bill of Rights was an historic statute that emerged from the “Glorious Revolution” of 1688-89, which culminated in the exile of King James II and the accession to the throne of William of Orange and Mary.

q: In what year was the English Bill of Rights passed into law?
explain: The Bill of Rights (1689) turned much of the Declaration of Rights accepted by William and Mary into statute; Parliament passed it in December 1689.

sources.title: United Kingdom - Revolution, 1688, Glorious | Britannica
sources.quote: The Bill of Rights (1689), a more conservative document than even the declaration, was passed into law, and it established the principle that only a Protestant could wear the crown of England.

sources.title: The Convention and Bill of Rights - UK Parliament
sources.quote: The rights affirmed in the Declaration did, however, take statutory effect in December 1689 when the Convention, with William and Mary's royal assent, passed the Declaration as an Act of Parliament, now known as the Bill of Rights.

q: In what year was Isaac Newton's Principia first published?
explain: Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in London in 1687, set out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.

sources.title: Principia | Britannica
sources.quote: The Principia was published in 1687 and is considered one of the most important works in the history of modern science.

sources.title: Principia. | Library of Congress
sources.quote: The Principia appeared in three editions during Newton's lifetime: the first in 1687, with a print run of 300--400 copies

q: Which English physician published De motu cordis in 1628, describing the circulation of the blood?
explain: Harvey's De motu cordis (1628) argued that the heart pumps blood around the body through a single system of arteries and veins.
hook: Harvey's heart: blood goes round and round.

sources.title: William Harvey - Circulation, Anatomy, Physiology | Britannica
sources.quote: Harvey’s key work was Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus ( Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals ), published in 1628, with an English version in 1653. Harvey’s greatest achievement was to recognize that the blood flows rapidly around the human body , being pumped through a single system of arteries and veins

sources.title: Ceaseless motion: William Harvey’s experimentations in circulation | RCP Museum
sources.quote: In 1628, after 10 years of painstaking solitary research, Harvey at last published his discovery in a book, known as De motu cordis . His idea, that blood is pumped around the body by the heart in a state of ceaseless motion, proved highly controversial to some

q: On what date did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
explain: Congress adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776; the engrossed parchment copy was signed starting August 2, 1776.

sources.title: Declaration of Independence (1776) | National Archives
sources.quote: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. It was engrossed on parchment and on August 2, 1776, delegates began signing it.

sources.title: Creating the Declaration: A Timeline | National Archives
sources.quote: Late in the morning of July 4, the Declaration was officially adopted, and the "Committee of Five" took the manuscript copy of the document to John Dunlap, official printer to the Congress.

q: In what year was the Treaty of Paris signed, ending the American Revolution?
explain: Signed on September 3, 1783, the treaty ended the war and had Britain formally recognize the United States as independent.

sources.title: Treaty of Paris (1783) | National Archives
sources.quote: This treaty, signed on September 3, 1783, between the American colonies and Great Britain, ended the American Revolution and formally recognized the United States as an independent nation.

sources.title: Treaty of Paris, 1783 - Office of the Historian
sources.quote: France signed preliminary articles of peace with Great Britain on January 20, 1783, followed by a formal peace of Paris signed on September 3, 1783.

q: On what date did Parisians storm the Bastille?
explain: The storming of the Bastille, a Paris fortress-prison seen as a symbol of royal tyranny, is commemorated each year as Bastille Day, France's national holiday.

sources.title: Storming of the Bastille | Britannica
sources.quote: On July 14, 1789, a crowd of Parisians stormed the Bastille , a medieval fortress and state prison, fearing King Louis XVI would suppress the newly formed National Assembly.

sources.title: French Revolution | Timeline | Britannica
sources.quote: The storming of the Bastille prison on July 14, 1789, was one of the opening events of the French Revolution.

q: In what year was King Louis XVI of France executed?
explain: Convicted by the National Convention, Louis XVI was guillotined in the Place de la Revolution in Paris on January 21, 1793.

sources.title: Louis XVI | Britannica
sources.quote: He was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution in Paris on January 21, 1793.

sources.title: Procès et exécution de Louis XVI - Assemblée nationale
sources.quote: Le 21 janvier 1793 à 10 h 22, place de la Révolution (actuelle place de la Concorde), la guillotine s’abat sur le corps du roi.

q: Which revolutionary leader oversaw the Reign of Terror and was executed in July 1794?
explain: Robespierre was overthrown in the National Convention on July 27, 1794 and executed the next day, which marked the end of the Reign of Terror.

sources.title: French Revolution | Timeline | Britannica
sources.quote: The Reign of Terror is overseen by Maximilien Robespierre . ... Robespierre is overthrown in the National Convention. He is executed the next day, signaling the end of the Reign of Terror.

sources.title: The French Revolution: Phases and Dates - UC Santa Barbara
sources.quote: July 28, 1794 : " Thermidor :" Robespierre executed, end of terror.

q: In which Paris cathedral was Napoleon crowned emperor in December 1804?
explain: Napoleon's coronation took place at Notre-Dame de Paris on December 2, 1804, in the presence of Pope Pius VII.

sources.title: A close-up on: the coronation of Napoleon I - napoleon.org
sources.quote: On 2 December, 1804, the cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris was the stage on which the coronation of Napoleon I was played out, in the presence of Pope Pius VII.

sources.title: The McGill University Napoleon Collection - Timeline
sources.quote: 2 December (11 frimaire, an XIII). Coronation of Napoleon and Josephine at Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris .

q: Which pope was present at Napoleon's 1804 coronation, where Napoleon crowned himself?
explain: Pope Pius VII presided over the ceremony, but Napoleon broke with tradition by placing the crown on his own head and then crowning Josephine.

sources.title: A close-up on: the coronation of Napoleon I - napoleon.org
sources.quote: On 2 December, 1804, the cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris was the stage on which the coronation of Napoleon I was played out, in the presence of Pope Pius VII. The new emperor broke with tradition by crowning himself

sources.title: The Life of Napoleon Bonaparte - Timeline of Key Events | Museums Victoria
sources.quote: While the ceremony was officiated over by Pope Pius VII, Napoleon actually crowned himself and then Joséphine, thus rejecting the authority of the Church.

q: In what year was the Napoleonic Code (French Civil Code) enacted?
explain: The Code Civil des Francais was enacted on March 21, 1804, consolidating principles such as equality before the law and the abolition of feudalism; it is still in force in revised form.

sources.title: Napoleonic Code | Britannica
sources.quote: The Napoleonic Code is the French civil code enacted on March 21, 1804, and is still extant, with revisions.

sources.title: The McGill University Napoleon Collection - Timeline
sources.quote: 21 March (30 ventôse, an XII). Publication of the Civil Code .

q: In what year was the Battle of Waterloo, Napoleon's final defeat, fought?
explain: Fought on June 18, 1815 near Brussels, Waterloo ended 23 years of recurrent warfare between France and the other European powers.

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | Britannica
sources.quote: Battle of Waterloo , (June 18, 1815), Napoleon ’s final defeat, ending 23 years of recurrent warfare between France and the other powers of Europe .

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | National Army Museum
sources.quote: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 between Napoleon’s French Army and a coalition led by the Duke of Wellington and Marshal Blücher.

q: Which British commander led the allied army that defeated Napoleon at Waterloo?
explain: Wellington's coalition army, joined by Prussian forces under Blucher, defeated Napoleon at Waterloo on June 18, 1815.

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | Britannica
sources.quote: Fought near Waterloo village, Belgium, it pitted Napoleon’s 72,000 French troops against the duke of Wellington ’s army of 68,000 (British, Dutch, Belgian, and German soldiers) aided by 45,000 Prussians under Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher . Napoleon was defeated

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | National Army Museum
sources.quote: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 between Napoleon’s French Army and a coalition led by the Duke of Wellington and Marshal Blücher.

q: Which Prussian field marshal brought his army to support Wellington at Waterloo?
explain: Although beaten at Ligny two days earlier, Blucher's Prussians joined Wellington at Waterloo and their flank attack helped complete Napoleon's defeat.

sources.title: Napoleon’s defeat at the Battle of Waterloo and its aftermath | Britannica
sources.quote: The battle was fought near Waterloo village, south of Brussels, during the Hundred Days of Napoleon’s restoration, by Napoleon’s 72,000 troops against the duke of Wellington ’s combined Allied army of 68,000 aided by 45,000 Prussians under Gebhard von Blücher.

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | National Army Museum
sources.quote: Wellington’s army beats off a succession of French attacks. The arrival of the Prussians completes Napoleon’s defeat.

q: To which South Atlantic island was Napoleon exiled after Waterloo, where he died in 1821?
explain: After his second abdication in June 1815, Napoleon was exiled to remote St. Helena, where he died on May 5, 1821. (Elba was his first exile, in 1814.)

sources.title: Napoleon I | Britannica
sources.quote: In October 1815 Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of St. Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he remained until he died on May 5, 1821, at age 51.

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo | National Army Museum
sources.quote: He spent the rest of his life in exile on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic.

q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
explain: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century and spread from there to continental Europe, North America and beyond.

sources.title: Industrial Revolution | Britannica
sources.quote: This process began in Britain in the 18th century and from there spread to other parts of the world.

sources.title: Industrial Revolution | Key Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: The process began in Britain, where the Industrial Revolution was largely confined from the 1760s to the 1830s.

q: Which English inventor created the spinning jenny, patented in 1770?
explain: Hargreaves conceived the hand-powered spinning jenny about 1764; it let one worker spin several threads at once. Arkwright (water frame), Crompton (spinning mule) and Kay (flying shuttle) made other textile inventions.
hook: Jenny spins many threads at once.

sources.title: Spinning jenny | Britannica
sources.quote: Spinning jenny , early multiple-spindle machine for spinning wool or cotton , invented by James Hargreaves in England and patented in 1770.

sources.title: James Hargreaves | Britannica
sources.quote: James Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny about 1764 and patented it in 1770. ... Hargreaves’s invention also helped pave the way for other important advances in spinning technology , including Richard Arkwright’s water frame and Samuel Crompton’s spinning mule .

q: What device, conceived in 1765, was James Watt's key improvement to the Newcomen steam engine?
explain: By condensing steam in a chamber apart from the cylinder, Watt's separate condenser kept the cylinder hot and greatly cut fuel use; he patented it in 1769.

sources.title: James Watt | Britannica
sources.quote: In 1765 Watt conceived of a separate condenser—a device to reduce the amount of waste produced by the Newcomen steam engine. Watt patented the device in 1769.

sources.title: Watt's second separate condenser, 1765 | Science Museum Group Collection
sources.quote: Early Newcomen engines were inefficient as their working cycle entailed continual heating and cooling of the cylinder, which wasted fuel. The separate condenser meant the steam was condensed in a separate chamber, allowing the cylinder to be kept hot and greatly increasing fuel efficiency.

q: The Confederate attack on which fort in April 1861 began the American Civil War?
explain: Confederate batteries opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, on April 12, 1861; the Union garrison surrendered and the war formally began.

sources.title: Civil War Timeline - Gettysburg National Military Park (NPS)
sources.quote: April 12, 1861- Confederate forces fire upon Fort Sumter, South Carolina . The Civil War formally begins.

sources.title: Battle of Fort Sumter | Britannica
sources.quote: The Battle of Fort Sumter , which took place April 12–14, 1861, was the opening engagement of the American Civil War.

q: In what year did Abraham Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation (effective January 1)?
explain: Issued January 1, 1863, it declared that all persons held as slaves within the rebellious areas "are, and henceforward shall be free."

sources.title: Emancipation Proclamation (1863) | National Archives
sources.quote: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, announcing, "that all persons held as slaves" within the rebellious areas "are, and henceforward shall be free."

sources.title: Transcript of the Proclamation | National Archives
sources.quote: Done at the City of Washington, this first day of January, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty three

q: On what date did Lincoln deliver the Gettysburg Address?
explain: Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, months after the battle of July 1-3, 1863.

sources.title: Today in History - November 19 | Library of Congress
sources.quote: On November 19 , 1863, President Abraham Lincoln delivered a short speech at the close of ceremonies dedicating the battlefield cemetery at Gettysburg , Pennsylvania.

sources.title: Civil War Timeline - Gettysburg National Military Park (NPS)
sources.quote: November 19, 1863- Dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg. President Abraham Lincoln delivers the Gettysburg Address.

q: Who led the 1860 Expedition of the Thousand that conquered Sicily?
explain: Garibaldi's volunteers landed at Marsala on May 11, 1860 and conquered Sicily in under three months, overthrowing the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

sources.title: Expedition of the Thousand | Britannica
sources.quote: Expedition of the Thousand , campaign undertaken in 1860 by Giuseppe Garibaldi that overthrew the Bourbon Kingdom of the  Two Sicilies (Naples) and permitted the union of southern Italy and Sicily with the north.

sources.title: Italy - Garibaldi, Thousand, Unification | Britannica
sources.quote: Despite scant preparations and a shortage of weapons, Garibaldi’s volunteers landed at Marsala on May 11, 1860, and in less than three months conquered the entire island of Sicily.

q: Who became the first king of Italy when the kingdom was proclaimed in 1861?
explain: Victor Emmanuel II, king of Piedmont-Sardinia, was proclaimed king of Italy on March 17, 1861; he kept the numeral II to show continuity with the kingdom of Sardinia.

sources.title: Piedmont-Sardinia - Countries - Office of the Historian
sources.quote: When the King of Piedmont-Sardinia, Victor Emmanuel II , was proclaimed King of Italy on March 17, 1861, George Perkins Marsh was appointed U.S. Minister to the King of Italy at Turin on April 26, 1861.

sources.title: Unification of Italy - Piedmont in 1850 | Britannica
sources.quote: In March 1861 the parliament declared Victor Emmanuel to be king of Italy—his title remained Victor Emmanuel II, to show that it was no new state but a continuation of the old kingdom of Sardinia.

q: Which Piedmontese statesman engineered Italian unification and became the first prime minister of the Kingdom of Italy?
explain: Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont from 1852, used international rivalries to unify Italy under the House of Savoy in 1861; he died in June 1861.

sources.title: Camillo Benso, count di Cavour | Britannica
sources.quote: Camillo Benso, count di Cavour (born August 10, 1810, Turin , Piedmont, French Empire—died June 6, 1861, Turin, Italy) was a Piedmontese statesman, a conservative whose exploitation of international rivalries and of revolutionary movements brought about the unification of Italy (1861) under the House of Savoy , with himself as the first prime minister of the new kingdom.

sources.title: 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/Cavour, Camillo Benso, Count - Wikisource
sources.quote: By the 4th of November he was prime minister, a position which he held with two short interruptions until his death.

q: In which French palace was the German Empire proclaimed in January 1871?
explain: On January 18, 1871, near the end of the Franco-Prussian War, Bismarck read the proclamation of the German Empire in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

sources.title: Proclamation of the German Empire, 1871 | Château de Versailles
sources.quote: The Confederation was dissolved on the 20th, and the proclamation of the Empire was set to be delivered on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors .

sources.title: German Empire - Franco-Prussian War, Unification, Bismarck | Britannica
sources.quote: He was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles on January 18, 1871.

q: Which king of Prussia was proclaimed the first German emperor in 1871?
explain: King William I of Prussia (king from 1861) was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles on January 18, 1871, with Bismarck as chancellor.

sources.title: German Empire | Britannica
sources.quote: The first German Emperor was William I , who was proclaimed as such on January 18, 1871, in Versailles. Prior to this, he was the King of Prussia from 1861.

sources.title: Proclamation of the German Empire, 1871 | Château de Versailles
sources.quote: After the Te Deum the proclamation was read out by Bismarck, dressed in a cuirassier uniform. At the end the Grand Duke of Bade cried: “Long live His Majesty Emperor Wilhelm!”
